newsitem.title: UK: Global Ocean Carriers aims to operate 25 ships.
newsitem.headline: Global Ocean Carriers aims to operate 25 ships.

text.p: New York-listed shipping group Global Ocean Carriers Ltd said Thursday that its long term aim is to operate up 25 vessels.
Global Ocean executive vice president Michael Jolliffe outlined the company's long term plans as he addressed potential investors for the group's imminent issue of $125 million in senior notes.
Speaking in London, Jolliffe said: "The long term goal is to develop Global Ocean carriers into a $500 million company operating 20 to 25 vessels."
The current bond issue is aimed at funding the $55 million purchase of four new vessels and paying off $61.5 million existing debts.
The additional ships will increase Global Ocean's fleet to 12 ships.
With the additional ships, Global Ocean forecasts that profits will increase to $23.9 million, from $9.3 million in 1996, as revenues rise to $44 million from $22.9 million.

Global also aims longer term to issue more equity. There are currently 3.8 million shares in the company which Joiffe said has a net asset value of around $6 per share but currently trades at aroud $3 per share due to lack of liquidity.
Jolliffe said the company would soon sell off its remaining products carrier as it focused on container ship feeder operations but retained a presence in the dry bulk market.
He said Global Ocean was using the current issue to help it reach a critical size to take advantage of consolidation among the major containership groups.

The top 20 container lines operate main haul service to major ports with large ships - carrying up to 6,000 containers - while feedership operators like Global use smaller vessels to transport containers from the main hub terminals to smaller regional ports.
"We are sub-contractors to the liner industry and some 44 percent of the world's feeder market is in south east Asia where Global Ocean's ships trade," Jolliffe said.
Jolliffe said the company saw itself being 70 percent positioned in the containership markets where stable growth of 11 percent a year has been achieved over the last decade.
Global Ocean would retain a limited position in the more volatile dry bulk markets where large profits could be made by buying ships now when the market was near historical lows.

The proceeds from the notes' issue will allow Global Ocean to pay for two 15 year old feeder ships, of 1,500 and 1,900 teu (containers are designated in twenty foot equivalent units) and two mid 1980s-built panamax bulk carriers. All the ships have been acquired from Tsakos Shipping of Greece, which manages its fleet.

Jolliffe said two charters with Neptune Orient Lines Ltd on its existing 2,340 teu container ships NOL Amber and NOL Crystal would earn $7.5 million income a year. That would pay off a large proportion of the $10.9 million interest on the bond issue over the next five years, he said.
It would sell the 1973-built panamax bulker Global Adelaide and 1973-built handymax Global Jane within the next two years, Jolliffe said.

Global Ocean's affiliation to Tsakos Shipping, one of the top five privately owned Greek shipping companies, also gave it economies of scale in buying stores and crew training facilities it could not afford on its own, he said.

The links with Tsakos allowed Global Ocean to operate its vessels at lower cost than competitors, Jolliffe said, and the fact that the company was Liberian-registered company and based in Athens meant it did not have to pay tax.
